## Three outbreaks, the same problems

- COVID-19, 2020. $R_t$, the number of new infections per infected
  person, daily for thousands of locations. Weekly to SPI-M-O, the
  UK's modelling advisory group
- mpox, 2022. Nowcasting for UKHSA. Nowcasting is estimating what has
  already happened but has not yet been reported
- Bundibugyo virus disease, DRC, 2026. One joint model across five data
  streams, refit on every push
- Each time the methods from the last outbreak were not reusable, the
  models did not fit the data sources, and the data changed under us

![](../figures/exchange-timeline.png){width="62%" fig-align="center"
fig-alt="A timeline from 1760 to 2026. Small grey ticks for Bernoulli,
Ross, Kermack and McKendrick, foot and mouth and H1N1, then a grey dot
for Ebola in West Africa in 2014 labelled watching, and teal dots for
COVID-19 in 2020 labelled doing it, mpox in 2022 labelled nowcasting,
and Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC in 2026 labelled
live."}

::: {.attribution}
Abbott et al. 2020, Wellcome Open Research · Overton et al. 2023, PLoS
Comput Biol · [BVDOutbreakSize][bvd] · dates in
`notes/research-history.md`, `scripts/keynote-timeline.py`
:::

## Joint models from reusable parts

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Models that use several data sources at once give better evidence
  than chains of separate models. Building one during an outbreak is
  slow, and needs several kinds of expertise
- So, components that combine into joint models with the uncertainty
  carried through. Delays first, then infections and observation
- And a written workflow for adding data sources one at a time, with
  the feedback loops drawn in
- In R and Stan first. In Julia now
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-workflow-lego.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Four columns of building blocks. Process models: three renewal
variants. Observation models: eight ways to link infections to counts,
with delays and ascertainment. Inference and computation choices, from
HMC to synthetic likelihood. Data integration choices, from ensembling
to full joint modelling. The four snap together at the bottom right."}

::: {.attribution}
Figure 6 of Abbott et al., [A workflow for infectious disease
modelling][wf] · [epiaware.org](https://epiaware.org) · Lison et al.
2024, PLoS Comput Biol
:::
:::
::::

## Where the tools get used

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Consulting time with CDC collaborators, UKHSA, and state and local
  public health in the US. The aim is to add other countries' public
  health departments
- In outbreaks. `epidist` in the DRC response's NEJM correspondence
  this August. Several teams using the tools in Exercise Pegasus, the
  UK's 2025 national pandemic exercise
- Next, tools flexible and extensible enough that a language model can
  drive them
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-public-health-use.png){width="100%"

## epiforecasts and the epinowcast community

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- epiforecasts, led by Sebastian Funk at LSHTM. Real-time modelling and
  evaluating it. `EpiNow2`, `scoringutils`, the European COVID-19
  Forecast Hub from 2021, now ECDC's RespiCast
- 2020 to 2022, weekly $R_t$ estimates and forecasts to SPI-M-O
- epinowcast. A forum of over 50 researchers and public health analysts,
  and a monthly seminar since May 2023, 31 so far
- Community >> methods or models alone

::: {.attribution}
[github.com/epiforecasts](https://github.com/epiforecasts) ·
